jeongsiScore.title: Jeongsi Converted Score Calculator
jeongsiScore.subtitle: Enter your CSAT scores and the scoring formula from a university's admissions guide to get its converted score. Save formulas for your Ga, Na and Da group choices and compare them at once.

scores.title: My CSAT scores
scores.desc: Enter the standard scores and percentiles from your score report. Before the report arrives on December 11, use values estimated from your self-graded answers. The scores shown at first are examples.

pct.name: Percentile, equal weights
pct.desc: Example that weights Korean, Math, English and Inquiry 25% each using percentiles. English uses a grade conversion table (grade 1 = 100) inside the ratio, and Korean History adds bonus points by grade.

hum.name: Standard score, humanities
hum.desc: Example that weights Korean 40%, Math 30% and Inquiry 30% using standard scores. English is outside the ratio and deducts points from grade 2 down; Korean History adds bonus points.

sci.name: Standard score, sciences
sci.desc: Example that weights Korean 20%, Math 35%, English 15% and Inquiry 30% using standard scores, with a 5% bonus for Calculus/Geometry and for science subjects. Korean History adds bonus points.

formula.title: University formula
formula.desc: Copy the 'CSAT scoring method' table from the admissions guide of the university you plan to apply to. Formulas can differ between departments of the same university.
formula.templateNote: The examples are not any specific university's formula. Pick one, then adjust the ratios and tables to match the admissions guide.
formula.customDesc: This formula was edited from an example. Tap an example above to restore its original values.
formula.ratioHintIn: Korean, Math, English and Inquiry weights should add up to 100%.
formula.ratioHintAdd: English is added to or deducted from the total separately, so Korean, Math and Inquiry weights should add up to 100%.
formula.bonusHint: A bonus multiplies that area's score (5% means ×1.05). The science bonus applies per subject. The full score is the total split by the area weights, excluding English points and Korean History bonus.
formula.baseCta: Replace with the reference score in the admissions guide
formula.baseHint: Each standard score is divided by this value before the weight is applied. The defaults (150 for Korean and Math, 80 per inquiry subject) are rough values near recent CSAT top standard scores. This year's top scores are released with the official results on December 11. Use them if the guide divides by each area's top score, or the fixed value (such as 200) if it uses one.
formula.basePct: Percentiles are out of 100, so there is nothing to change.
formula.advanced: English and Korean History grade tables
formula.engTableHintRatio: Enter the English conversion table from the guide. The highest value counts as full marks before the English weight is applied.
formula.engTableHintAdd: These points are added to the total as is. Enter deductions as negative numbers, such as -3.
formula.histTableHint: Added to the total as is. Use negative numbers for deductions, or all zeros if it is not used.

howTo.title: How to use
items: Enter standard scores and percentiles for Korean, Math and Inquiry, plus your English and Korean History grades, from your score report or self-graded estimate.
Pick an example formula, then change the score basis, weights, English method, bonuses and full score to match the admissions guide.
Open 'English and Korean History grade tables' and fill in all nine grades from the guide.
Save with a name and group to compare up to six formulas with the same scores. Copying the link keeps both your scores and the current formula.

findFormula.title: Finding the formula in the admissions guide
items: Open the university's '2027 regular admission (jeongsi) guide' on its admissions site and look for the 'CSAT scoring method' or 'CSAT weights' table.
Check the area weights, score basis (standard score, percentile or converted standard score) and number of inquiry subjects for your department (humanities, sciences, arts and so on).
The English conversion table, Korean History bonus (or deduction) table and Math/science bonus rules are usually in tables further down the same section.
Adiga (adiga.kr) also lists jeongsi information by university. After scores are released, many universities open an official converted score calculator on their admissions site.

model.title: How this calculator works
items: Area points = weight × (percentile ÷ 100, or standard score ÷ reference maximum) × full score
Inquiry uses the average of two subjects (the same as their sum divided by the sum of reference scores), or the better subject after bonuses.
With English inside the ratio, the grade's table value is divided by the table's highest value. With add/deduct, the table value is added to the total as is.
Total = Korean, Math, Inquiry (and English) points + English points + Korean History bonus. Calculations keep full precision; results are shown to two decimal places.
Formulas that choose areas, such as giving more weight to the better of Korean or Math or using only the top three areas, are not supported yet.

items.q: Should I use standard scores or percentiles?
items.a: Use whatever the university specifies in the 'score basis' column of its guide. A standard score shows how far your raw score is from the average (mean 100 for Korean and Math, 50 for inquiry), so the top score rises when the exam is harder. A percentile is the share of test takers who scored below you (0-100). Many top universities use standard scores, and many others use percentiles.

items.q: Where do I enter converted standard scores?
items.a: Inquiry subjects differ in difficulty, so raw standard scores can favor some subjects. Many universities therefore build their own converted standard score table from percentiles. Once a university publishes its table after scores are released, enter that value in the inquiry standard score field and set the inquiry reference maximum to that table's highest value.

items.q: Why are there two English methods?
items.a: English is graded on an absolute scale, so you only get a grade. Some universities convert grades to points (for example, grade 1 = 100, grade 2 = 95) and weight them like other areas. Others leave English out of the ratio and add or deduct points by grade. Choose 'Inside the ratio' if the weight table has an English column, and 'Add/deduct points' if English is listed as a separate bonus or deduction.

Korean History is also graded on an absolute scale. Most universities give full bonus points down to a certain grade and slightly fewer below that. Enter the guide's points for all nine grades; use negative numbers if it is a deduction.

items.q: How are science and Calculus bonuses calculated?
items.a: Many science-track departments give a bonus to students who took Calculus or Geometry, or science inquiry subjects. This calculator multiplies the area's score by the bonus (5% means ×1.05) before applying the weight. The science bonus applies per subject, and with 'Best 1 subject' the bonus is applied before choosing the better one. Universities differ in what the bonus applies to (standard score, percentile or converted score) and in what order, so results may differ slightly.

items.q: What is the reference maximum, and why 150 and 80?
items.a: It is the value a standard score is divided by before weighting. Depending on the university, it may be that year's top standard score per area, a fixed value such as 200, or the top converted standard score. The defaults are rough values near recent CSAT top scores, so replace them with this year's top scores or the guide's reference values once official results are released on December 11. Percentiles are always out of 100.

items.q: Why is my result different from the university's calculator?
items.a: Universities differ in the details: converted standard scores for inquiry, fixed reference values instead of top scores, rounding (when and how decimals are rounded or truncated), extra weight on the better of Korean or Math, and when bonuses are applied. This calculator is for rough scores and comparing formulas while reading guides. Always confirm your final score with the university's own calculator before applying.

items.q: Can I trust a score calculated before results are released?
items.a: Scores for the 2027 CSAT are released on December 11, 2026. Until then you are entering standard scores and percentiles estimated from self-graded answers, so the result may differ from your real score. Use it to gauge your range for now, and recalculate with your actual scores and this year's reference maximums once you get your report.

Up to six formulas are stored in this browser's local storage and are never sent to a server. To use one on another device, load it and copy the link: the page opens with your scores and that formula. Clearing browser data also deletes saved formulas.

items.q: Does a higher converted score mean better chances?
items.a: No. Each university has its own full score, formula and cutoff, so converted scores cannot be compared across universities. Compare each score with that university's admitted students' scores from last year, available on Adiga or the university's admissions site.
